newsitem.title: USA: U.S. denies new TWA "friendly fire" charge.
newsitem.headline: U.S. denies new TWA "friendly fire" charge.

text.p: Nearly four months after a TWA jet exploded near New York, killing 230 people, the U.S. government on Friday denied new charges that a Navy missile accidentally shot down the plane.

"The United States military did not shoot a missile at this airplane," a visibly angry James Kallstrom, head of the FBI in New York, told a news conference in New York. He said the so-called friendly fire theory was "total, unadulterated nonsense."
"Nothing, nothing like that has taken place, would take place, would ever take place under any circumstances."

The latest version of an alleged coverup conspiracy theory that has circulated on the Internet and in other media for months erupted at a time when some investigators were leaning toward ruling out a bomb or missile and declaring the July 17 disaster an accident.

A report in Friday's Washington Post quoted a senior National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) official as saying if no evidence of a bomb or missile is found in the remaining scraps of the Boeing 747 on the ocean floor, the agency will declare the crash an accident.

Sparking the latest speculation that the military shot down Paris-bound TWA Flight 800 was former White House press secretary Pierre Salinger, who said on Thursday in France that he had been given a government document that he believed proved a U.S. missile destroyed the jet.
But on Friday, Salinger said he was told it had been on the Internet for two months and acknowledged his information was at least second-hand.

Salinger's comments were "unfortunate and irresponsible," Jim Hall, head of the NTSB, said at the news conference with the FBI. Hall criticised Salinger "not only for causing consternation and pain to families of the victims but also for the fact that a once well-respected journalist would seize information he now admits was third-hand at best and try to promote it as some scoop of his."
Another NTSB official said the agency had been flooded with calls from victims' families, whom he described as being "in very severe pain" after Salinger's comments.
Kallstrom said investigators had studied the possibility of so-called friendly fire and concluded "the military of this country had nothing to do with this horrendous tragedy."

Navy Rear Adm. Edward Kristensen said a P-3 "Orion" patrol aircraft was on a routine training flight about 80 miles (130 km) southwest of the crash site and flew to the scene to help in recovery efforts. It had dropped 39 sonar buoys during its flight, all of which were accounted for, he said.

The USS Normandy cruiser, about 185 miles (300 km) away, was using such low power that its limited radar range did not detect Flight 800, he said. The cruiser carried surface-to-air missiles, all of which were still on board, he said.
The FBI and NTSB have identified three possible causes of the disaster -- a bomb, a missile or catastrophic mechanical failure -- but have not reached any definitive conclusion.
"We don't know which one of those theories caused this tragedy," Kallstrom repeated on Friday.

The Washington Post quoted the NTSB's director of aviation safety Bernard Loeb as saying: "If we find no evidence of criminal activity in anything else we retrieve, as far as I am concerned this will be an airplane accident and we will treat it as such."
Investigators believe the centre fuel tank exploded but do not know what caused the blast.

Salinger, 71, press spokesman for President John Kennedy and later Paris bureau chief for ABC, told French media on Friday that the document blaming a missile for the crash had been on the Internet for two months.

He acknowledged he had received the document, which he initially said came from a U.S. Secret Service agent, second-hand from an unidentified Frenchman "involved in various government things" who had met a U.S. agent.

The U.S. Secret Service said it had "absolutely no information" that anyone with official ties to the Secret Service was connected to any such document. Kallstrom said he was baffled that Salinger had not contacted the agency first with his information if he believed it was authentic.

He added that investigators were encouraged by debris being dug up by trawlers now dredging the crash site but he said significant pieces of the jet's centre fuel tank and fuselage remained to be found.
